notes.meaning: Paul turns to a question the Corinthians had sent him about eating meat previously offered to idols in pagan temples. Some in the church bragged about their religious knowledge, but Paul warns that bare facts only make people proud. Love, on the other hand, strengthens others and builds up the church family.

Anyone who thinks he is an expert and looks down on others proves he is actually missing the point. Real knowledge is not just having facts in your head, but using them with humility and care for your neighbor. If someone lacks love, he has not yet learned how God wants him to think.

True knowledge begins with a heart that loves God, which naturally overflows into loving other believers. God welcomes, approves, and claims as His own the person who walks in this kind of love. Being known and loved by God is far more precious than merely having a lot of information.

Paul returns to the core question and agrees with the basic truth the Corinthians held. An idol made of wood or stone has no real divine life in it, and there is only one true God. Because these gods do not actually exist, the meat offered to them is not magically spoiled or made evil in itself.

Pagan culture worshiped countless gods, whether stars in the sky or emperors and rulers on the earth. People gave these statues, spirits, and heroes divine titles, calling them gods and lords. Yet Paul explains that these are only gods in human imagination, having no real divine power compared to the true Creator.

Christians hold to one true God, the Father, who created the entire universe and gave us life so we might live for Him. We also confess one Lord, Jesus Christ, who was the agent in creating all things and through whom we have new spiritual life. Believers belong completely to this one God, not to any imaginary pagan deity.

Even though mature believers understand that idols are nothing, not every Christian in Corinth has grasped this truth yet. Some new believers spent their whole lives worshiping idols, so eating that meat still feels to them like honoring a false god. When they eat it despite their inner doubts, they feel guilty and their weak conscience is wounded.

Paul points out that physical food has no power to change our standing before God. Eating meat does not earn favor with God, and skipping meat does not make us less holy. What truly matters to God is a clean and loving heart, not what is on our plates.

Believers have the freedom to eat, but they must handle that freedom with great caution. If exercising this freedom tempts a less-informed Christian to do something he thinks is wrong, that freedom has turned into a dangerous trap. Christian liberty must always be guided by love and care for others.

Paul pictures an informed believer dining right inside the dining hall of an idol temple, confident that the idol is nothing. A weaker Christian who sees this might be encouraged by that example to join in, even though he still feels it is an act of false worship. Instead of being built up in good, the weak brother is pushed to violate his own conscience.

When an informed believer insists on his rights, his selfish choice can ruin a fellow Christian. The weaker brother is led into the guilt and trap of idolatry by following an example he cannot follow in faith. Paul reminds everyone that Jesus loved this struggling brother enough to give His life on the cross for him.

differ.view: Christ died for all people, so a believer who is led back into sin through another's bad example can truly fall away and be lost forever.
Christ effectively saves all for whom He died, so destroying a brother refers to wrecking his conscience, spiritual peace, and growth, not losing his eternal salvation.

notes.meaning: Striking a blow against a fellow Christian's tender conscience is not just an unkind act against a person. Because believers are united to Jesus as members of His body, hurting them is an attack on the Savior Himself. Disregarding the spiritual well-being of another Christian is a direct sin against Christ.

Paul concludes by sharing his own personal rule of life. He would rather give up eating meat entirely than cause another believer to fall into sin and harm his walk with God. True love willingly surrenders its personal rights to protect and support others.
